## Upper bound: one target works whenever \(\delta(G)>n/5\)

They proved the stronger statement that **one fixed finite triangle-free graph** receives every eligible \(G\) with \(\delta(G)>n/5\).

The key intermediate object is a coloring with at most 36 colors such that adjacent vertices, and endpoints of every length-three walk, have different colors.

Choose a **maximum-cardinality** collection \(r_1,\ldots,r_s\) whose open neighborhoods \(B_i=N(r_i)\) are pairwise disjoint. Because each neighborhood has more than \(n/5\) vertices, \(s\leq4\). Define
\[
L(v)=\{i:N(v)\cap B_i\ne\varnothing\}.
\]
Every label is nonempty, by maximality. Adjacent vertices have disjoint labels: otherwise the corresponding walks through a common \(r_i\) produce a closed walk of length five, which in a simple graph entails a triangle or a five-cycle.

Let \(S_i=\{v:L(v)=\{i\}\}\). Any two vertices of \(S_i\) have intersecting neighborhoods. Otherwise their two disjoint neighborhoods could replace \(B_i\), increasing the packing. Consequently, no two vertices of \(S_i\) can be endpoints of a length-three walk: combining that walk with their common neighbor again gives a forbidden closed five-walk.

The remaining “core,” consisting of vertices with labels of size at least two, is bipartite. Indeed, edges require disjoint labels; on at most four indices, two such labels can be disjoint only when they are complementary two-element sets.

Color each \(S_i\) separately. Color a core vertex by its bipartition side together with the set of \(S_i\)'s it neighbors. This uses at most
\[
s+2\cdot2^s\leq36
\]
colors. It excludes monochromatic endpoints of length-three walks: a walk entirely in the core has opposite-side endpoints; if an internal vertex lies in some \(S_i\), equality of the endpoint signatures would produce a length-three walk between two vertices of \(S_i\).

From this coloring \(\phi\), construct a universal target with vertices
\[
(i,A),\qquad i\in[36],\quad A\subseteq[36]\setminus\{i\},
\]
and adjacency defined by
\[
(i,A)\sim(j,B)
\iff i\in B,\ j\in A,\ A\cap B=\varnothing.
\]
The map
\[
v\longmapsto\bigl(\phi(v),\{\phi(w):w\in N(v)\}\bigr)
\]
is a homomorphism. The length-three condition ensures disjoint neighbor-color sets across each edge. A triangle in the target is impossible: the first coordinate of its third vertex would belong to both sets attached to the other two vertices.

Thus the property holds for every \(c>1/5\), proving the upper bound on the infimum. This does not settle \(c=1/5\).

### High-chromatic seeds with nearly half-density independent covers

Let \(S(N,k)\) have increasing \(k\)-tuples as vertices, with consecutive overlapping windows adjacent. For fixed \(k\), its chromatic number is unbounded as \(N\) grows. A \(q\)-coloring induces a coloring of \(S(N,k-1)\) by sets of colors of right extensions, giving
\[
\chi(S(N,k-1))\leq2^{\chi(S(N,k))}.
\]
Iteration starts from \(S(N,1)=K_N\).

For even \(k\geq4\), each permutation of \([N]\) defines an independent set: select tuples whose permutation-largest entry occurs in position \(3,5,\ldots,k-1\). Adjacent windows cannot both qualify, because their common maximum shifts position by one. Counting all \(M=N!\) permutations, every vertex occurs in exactly
\[
r=M\frac{k-2}{2k}
\]
sets.

### Dense extension and obstruction

Orient the seed \(F=S(N,k)\), and replace each edge \(uv\) by
\[
u-x_{uv}-y_{uv}-v.
\]
Give these vertices types \(U,X,Y\), with labels \(u,u,v\), respectively.

For each type and each covering independent set, add \(W\) pads adjacent to precisely the base vertices of that type whose labels lie in that set. For each type, add another \(rW\) vertices, each adjacent to all \(MW\) pads of its family.

Writing \(b=|V(F)|+2|E(F)|\), the resulting graph satisfies
\[
n=b+3(M+r)W,\qquad \delta\geq rW.
\]

The crucial local lemma is that any length-three base walk with same-type endpoints has labels adjacent in \(F\). Therefore one pad cannot close such a walk into a five-cycle. Five-cycles with two pads would require an edge within one independent base type; cycles involving the added pad-only neighbors are excluded similarly. The base itself has girth at least nine. Triangles are also excluded by the type structure.

Choose \(\chi(F)>|V(H)|\). Any homomorphism to triangle-free \(H\) must send the original endpoints of every subdivided edge to different vertices: identifying them would create a closed three-walk in \(H\). Their images would therefore properly color \(F\), a contradiction.

Finally,
\[
\lim_{W\to\infty}\frac{rW}{n}
=\frac{k-2}{3(3k-2)}
\longrightarrow\frac19.
\]
For any \(c<1/9\), choose even \(k\) making this ratio exceed \(c\), then take
\[
W>\frac{cb}{r-3c(M+r)}.
\]
This disproves the property for every such \(c\).

## 4. Energy proof of the regularity lemma used above

Here are the details to make the upper argument independent of a regularity black box.

For a partition \(\mathcal P\), define its energy by
\[
\mathcal E(\mathcal P)=
\sum_{A,B\in\mathcal P}\frac{|A||B|}{n^2}d(A,B)^2.
\]
Regard every exceptional vertex as a singleton part. Then \(0\le\mathcal E\le1\), and refinement never decreases energy, by the weighted Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.

Start with \(m_0\) equal main clusters and fewer than \(m_0\) exceptional vertices. For sufficiently large \(n\), the exception has size at most \(\varepsilon n/2\).

If there are more than \(\varepsilon\ell^2\) irregular main-cluster pairs, choose witness subsets for each pair and split each cluster by all witnesses involving it. There are at most \(2^\ell\) resulting atoms per cluster.

For one irregular pair, its witness rectangle has relative weight at least \(\varepsilon^2\) and density differing from the old density by more than \(\varepsilon\). Its two ordered energy contributions therefore increase by at least
\[
2\varepsilon^4m^2/n^2.
\]
Summed over the irregular pairs, the increase is greater than
\[
2\varepsilon^5(\ell m/n)^2\ge\varepsilon^5,
\]
provided the exceptional set has size at most \(\varepsilon n\).

Let \(T=\lceil2\varepsilon^{-5}\rceil\). After splitting, equitize inside the atoms into blocks of size
\[
s=\left\lfloor\frac{\varepsilon n}{2T\ell2^\ell}\right\rfloor.
\]
Make every leftover vertex an exceptional singleton. This is still a refinement, so no energy is lost. At most
\[
\ell2^\ell s\le\frac{\varepsilon n}{2T}
\]
new vertices become exceptional per step.

If \(s\ge1\), the new number of clusters is at most
\[
\frac{4T\ell2^\ell}{\varepsilon}.
\]
Every old cluster retains at least one block, so the number remains at least \(m_0\). If \(s=0\), use the all-singleton partition; then
\[
n<\frac{2T\ell2^\ell}{\varepsilon},
\]
so its number of clusters is bounded as well.

There cannot be \(T\) energy-increasing failures, since energy is at most \(1\). The exceptional set remains at most
\[
\varepsilon n/2+T\cdot\varepsilon n/(2T)=\varepsilon n.
\]
The displayed recurrence bounds the final number of clusters solely in terms of \(\varepsilon,m_0\), proving the lemma.

from itertools import combinations, permutations, product
from math import factorial
import numpy as np


def shift_instance(N, k):
    assert N >= k >= 3 and k % 2 == 1

    vertices = list(combinations(range(N), k))
    index = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(vertices)}
    edges = [
        (index[t[:-1]], index[t[1:]])
        for t in combinations(range(N), k + 1)
    ]

    # Permutation-indexed independent cover.
    cover = [set() for _ in vertices]
    for j, pi in enumerate(permutations(range(N))):
        rank = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(pi)}
        for i, v in enumerate(vertices):
            pos = max(range(k), key=lambda s: rank[v[s]])
            if (pos + 1) % 2 == 0:
                cover[i].add(j)

    m = factorial(N)
    assert m * (k - 1) % (2 * k) == 0
    p = m * (k - 1) // (2 * k)
    assert all(len(s) == p for s in cover)
    assert all(not (cover[u] & cover[v]) for u, v in edges)

    # Three-subdivision, using nearest-endpoint labels.
    labels = [(0, i) for i in range(len(vertices))]
    core_edges = []
    for u, v in edges:
        a = len(labels)
        labels.extend([(1, u), (2, v)])
        core_edges.extend([(u, a), (a, a + 1), (a + 1, v)])

    z = len(labels)
    n = z + 3 * (m + p)  # L = 1
    adj = [set() for _ in range(n)]

    def add(u, v):
        assert u != v
        adj[u].add(v)
        adj[v].add(u)

    for u, v in core_edges:
        add(u, v)

    for typ in range(3):
        base = z + typ * (m + p)
        for i in range(m):
            for j in range(p):
                add(base + i, base + m + j)

    for u, (typ, label) in enumerate(labels):
        for i in cover[label]:
            add(u, z + typ * (m + p) + i)

    assert n == z + 3 * (m + p)
    assert min(map(len, adj)) >= p

    # Exact integer walk counts; these tested sizes cannot overflow int64.
    Delta = max(map(len, adj))
    assert n * Delta**5 < 2**63
    A = np.zeros((n, n), dtype=np.int64)
    for u in range(n):
        A[u, list(adj[u])] = 1
    B = A @ A
    C = B @ A
    assert np.trace(C) == 0       # No closed 3-walk.
    assert np.sum(B * C.T) == 0   # tr(A^5), no closed 5-walk.

    # Verify color-set descent, including empty extension sets.
    colors = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(vertices)}
    for j in range(k - 1, 0, -1):
        colors = {
            t: frozenset(
                colors[t + (y,)] for y in range(t[-1] + 1, N)
            )
            for t in combinations(range(N), j)
        }
        assert all(
            colors[t[:-1]] != colors[t[1:]]
            for t in combinations(range(N), j + 1)
        )
    assert len(set(colors.values())) == N

    return n, sum(map(len, adj)) // 2, min(map(len, adj))


def support_check(k=6):
    """Exhaust all reduced graphs and all admissible support triples."""
    pairs = list(combinations(range(k), 2))
    graphs = cases = 0

    for mask in range(1 << len(pairs)):
        adj = [0] * k
        for j, (u, v) in enumerate(pairs):
            if (mask >> j) & 1:
                adj[u] |= 1 << v
                adj[v] |= 1 << u
        if not all(adj):  # R must have no isolated vertex.
            continue
        graphs += 1

        neighborhood = [0] * (1 << k)
        for s in range(1, 1 << k):
            bit = s & -s
            neighborhood[s] = (
                neighborhood[s ^ bit] | adj[bit.bit_length() - 1]
            )

        for union in range(1, 1 << k):
            if union & neighborhood[union]:
                continue  # The union of the supports must be independent.

            vertices = [v for v in range(k) if (union >> v) & 1]
            # Each union vertex may belong to any nonempty set of supports.
            for memberships in product(range(1, 8), repeat=len(vertices)):
                S = [0, 0, 0]
                for v, membership in zip(vertices, memberships):
                    for i in range(3):
                        if (membership >> i) & 1:
                            S[i] |= 1 << v
                if not all(S):
                    continue

                T = [neighborhood[s] for s in S]
                if any(T[i] & T[j]
                       for i, j in combinations(range(3), 2)):
                    continue

                six = S + T
                assert all(six)
                assert all(
                    not (six[i] & six[j])
                    for i, j in combinations(range(6), 2)
                )
                assert sum(s.bit_count() for s in six) <= k
                cases += 1

    return graphs, cases


def universal_target(q):
    vertices = [
        (i, s)
        for i in range(q)
        for s in range(1 << q)
        if not ((s >> i) & 1)
    ]
    edges = set()

    for a, b in combinations(range(len(vertices)), 2):
        i, s = vertices[a]
        j, t = vertices[b]
        if ((t >> i) & 1) and ((s >> j) & 1) and not (s & t):
            edges.add((a, b))

    for triple in combinations(range(len(vertices)), 3):
        assert not all(
            tuple(sorted(e)) in edges
            for e in combinations(triple, 2)
        )
    return len(vertices), len(edges)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for N, k in [(4, 3), (5, 3)]:

    for q in range(1, 5):
        print("target", q, universal_target(q))
    print("six-set reduced graphs/cases", support_check())

## Conclusion

They established that the infimum is **\(1/9\)**:

- Every \(c>1/9\) has the required finite triangle-free target.

They did **not** determine whether the property holds at \(c=1/9\), which is unnecessary for computing the infimum. Nothing they found contradicts the supplied answer.

## Upper bound: every \(c>1/9\) works

Define \(J\) on \(V(G)\) by joining distinct vertices whenever a \(G\)-walk of length \(1\) or \(3\) connects them. The main task is to bound \(\chi(J)\) solely in terms of \(c\).

A \(q\)-coloring \(f\) of \(J\) gives an explicit triangle-free target \(W_q\). Its vertices are
\[
(i,S),\qquad i\in[q],\quad S\subseteq[q]\setminus\{i\},
\]
with adjacency defined by
\[
(i,S)\sim(j,T)\iff i\in T,\ j\in S,\ S\cap T=\varnothing.
\]
Map \(x\) to \((f(x),f(N_G(x)))\). For a \(G\)-edge \(xy\), the neighbor-color sets are disjoint because every neighbor of \(x\) and neighbor of \(y\) are connected by a three-edge walk. A triangle in \(W_q\) would force the first coordinate of its third vertex into the disjoint sets attached to its first two vertices. Thus \(W_q\) is triangle-free and has at most \(q2^{q-1}\) vertices.

### Regularity profiles and the nine-part obstruction

Set
\[
t=(9c-1)/1000,\qquad \varepsilon=t^2.
\]
Apply equitable regularity, then discard clusters with too many irregular partners. With sufficiently many initial clusters, the retained reduced graph \(R\), on \(k\) equal clusters, satisfies
\[
\delta(R)\ge(c-6t)k.
\]
Its edges represent regular pairs of density at least \(t\).

For each vertex \(v\), define its support \(S_v\) as the clusters in which \(v\) has at least \(t\) times the cluster size neighbors. At most \(4tn\) neighbors lie outside its support. Consequently, any profile class containing a \(J\)-edge has support size at least
\[
2(c-4t)k.
\]
Indeed, endpoints of a \(J\)-edge have disjoint \(G\)-neighborhoods: a common neighbor would produce a triangle or a \(5\)-cycle.

Regular-pair connector arguments establish:

1. Each \(S_v\) is independent in \(R\).
2. If \(xy\in E(G)\), then \(N_R(S_x)\cap N_R(S_y)=\varnothing\).
3. If \(x,z,y\) is a two-edge walk, no \(R\)-edge joins \(S_x\) to \(S_y\).

These follow by embedding respectively a triangle or a \(5\)-cycle if the stated restriction fails.

There are at most \(M=2^k\) profiles. If a profile class \(p\) had chromatic number greater than \(2^{M^2}\) in \(J\), color each of its \(J\)-edges by the ordered profiles \((q,r)\) of a chosen witness
\[
x-a-b-y.
\]
One edge-color subgraph must be nonbipartite. Any orientation of a nonbipartite graph contains a directed two-edge path, yielding a witness chain
\[
p-q-r-p-q-r-p.
\]
Thus all three profiles contain \(J\)-edges, and the chain supplies every required edge and two-edge relation between their types.

The connector restrictions imply that the following six sets are pairwise disjoint:
\[
S_p,S_q,S_r,\quad N_R(S_p),N_R(S_q),N_R(S_r).
\]
The first three each have size at least \(2(c-4t)k\); the latter three each have size at least \((c-6t)k\). Hence
\[
k\ge(9c-42t)k>k,
\]
a contradiction. Therefore
\[
\chi(J)\le M\,2^{M^2},
\]
uniformly in \(n\). Small graphs excluded by regularity’s size requirements are handled by adding finitely many triangle-free components to the target.

They also supplied an energy-increment proof of regularity: exceptional vertices remain singleton partition parts, so equitization inside refined atoms loses no energy. This closes the standard-lemma dependency.

## Lower bound: every \(c<1/9\) fails

Fix a finite triangle-free \(H\), and put \(h=\max(1,|V(H)|)\).

Use the shift graph \(F=S(N,k)\), where \(k\ge3\) is odd: vertices are increasing \(k\)-tuples, with edges between consecutive overlapping tuples from an increasing \((k+1)\)-tuple.

Two elementary facts supply the construction:

- A \(q\)-coloring of \(S(N,j)\) gives a \(2^q\)-coloring of \(S(N,j-1)\), by assigning each tuple the set of colors of its extensions. Iterating down to \(S(N,1)=K_N\) proves \(\chi(F)>h\) for sufficiently large \(N\).
- For each permutation \(\pi\), take tuples whose \(\pi\)-largest element occupies an even position. This is independent. Each tuple belongs to exactly
  \[
  p=\frac{(k-1)N!}{2k}
  \]
  of these \(m=N!\) independent sets. Write its permutation-label set as \(I_u\); adjacent labels have disjoint sets.

Replace every oriented edge \(u\to v\) by \(u-a_{uv}-b_{uv}-v\), obtaining \(X\). Give these vertices types \(0,1,2\) and labels \(u,u,v\). Same-type endpoints of any three-edge \(X\)-walk have adjacent labels.

Add three disjoint bicliques \(K_{mL,pL}\). In biclique \(i\), index the large side by permutations and \(L\) copies. Attach each type-\(i\) vertex with label \(u\) to the copies indexed by \(I_u\). Then
\[
n=|X|+3(m+p)L,\qquad \delta(G)\ge pL,
\]
and
\[
\frac{p}{3(m+p)}=\frac{k-1}{3(3k-1)}\longrightarrow\frac19.
\]
Choose \(k\), then \(L\), to obtain \(\delta(G)\ge cn\).

A complete cycle classification excludes triangles and \(5\)-cycles: \(X\) has girth at least nine; biclique-side vertices cannot participate; and remaining mixed \(5\)-cycles would require either a same-type \(X\)-edge or intersecting label sets of adjacent labels.

Finally, \(G\to H\) would properly color \(F\) with at most \(h\) colors: identifying endpoints of a subdivided edge would create a closed three-edge walk in \(H\), hence a triangle. Contradiction.
